Laboratory-reared cohorts of Eubosmina coregoni revealed that neonates emerge from the brood chamber at a total length at birth of 0.025 centimeters [Lb = 0.025 centimeters], a value derived from the diameter of subitaneous eggs produced by ovigerous females. This minute size at release is typical of many small-bodied cladocerans and reflects a reproductive strategy centered on producing numerous, relatively yolk-poor offspring. The earliest actively feeding juveniles begin filtering phytoplankton almost immediately after release, initiating a rapid phase of somatic growth that continues until the onset of sexual maturation. Field-collected specimens from temperate lakes during summer months indicate that individuals typically attain their ultimate total length of 0.08 centimeters [Li = 0.08 centimeters], a size that defines the asymptotic body dimension for this species under prevailing thermal and food regimes. This maximum length was confirmed through repeated measurements of post-pubertal adults maintained under optimal laboratory conditions, providing a reliable benchmark for comparative life-history studies.

The transition from the juvenile crustacean to the reproductively viable organism is marked by the attainment of a distinct size threshold. Specifically, puberty in Eubosmina coregoni is first observed when an individual reaches a total length at puberty of 0.042 centimeters [Lp = 0.042 centimeters], which corresponds to the onset of gametogenesis and the development of the first clutch of eggs within the brood pouch. This length threshold is a critical life-history milestone, as it signals the shift from exclusive investment in somatic growth to the allocation of resources toward reproductive effort. Individuals falling below this size have never been observed carrying eggs, confirming its utility as a diagnostic marker of physiological maturity. The consistency of this measurement across multiple lake populations suggests a strong genetic determination of the pubertal size, likely shaped by selective pressures balancing early reproduction against the survival costs of breeding at a smaller body size.

Experimental work conducted at a stable water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] allowed for precise quantification of the species' maximum reproductive output. Under these conditions, female Eubosmina coregoni were observed to produce, on average, 7 eggs in a single clutch [N_R_i = 7 eggs in a single clutch], and they completed approximately 1.4 clutches over the course of a single day [F_R_i = approximately 1.4 clutches over the course of a single day]. This represents an extraordinarily high daily reproductive rate for a cladoceran of this body size, likely facilitated by the rapid embryonic development that occurs within the brood chamber at this thermal regime. The availability of abundant algal food resources in the experimental vessels ensured that females were not energy-limited, allowing expression of their full physiological reproductive potential. Such a high fecundity and rapid brood turnover are adaptive in ephemeral pond habitats, enabling populations to rebound quickly from environmental perturbations.

Measurements of the ultimate dry weight, obtained from a sample of fully grown, non-ovigerous adult females, produced a mean value of 13 micrograms . This body mass, determined after desiccation to constant weight, is consistent with the allometric scaling relationships observed across the genus Eubosmina, where ultimate length and mass are tightly coupled. The dry mass provides a more ecologically meaningful metric than wet weight when comparing energy storage across populations, as it excludes the variable water content associated with reproductive tissues and gut contents. This value of 13 micrograms  serves as a key parameter for estimating individual contributions to secondary production and for parameterizing growth models that link body size to metabolic demand in freshwater zooplankton communities.

Longevity studies conducted in controlled laboratory aquaria at a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] determined that the maximum lifespan of Eubosmina coregoni is 140 days [am = 140 days]. This lifespan was recorded for individuals that were isolated from predators and supplied with abundant food, representing the physiological upper boundary of survival for this species. In natural lake environments, the realized lifespan is likely substantially shorter due to predation by fish and invertebrate planktivores, as well as seasonal fluctuations in resource availability. The value of 140 days [am = 140 days] at this specific temperature places Eubosmina coregoni among the longer-lived members of the Bosminidae, potentially reflecting a life-history strategy that balances sustained reproductive output over several weeks against the risks of mortality in a variable pelagic environment at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C].
